articles.title: Wu Shicun on why Beijing will not rule out Scarborough Shoal construction
articles.summary:
• Wu Shicun, founding president of China's National Institute for South China Sea Studies, argues that the Philippines' "assertive transparency" campaign deliberately provokes Chinese responses at disputed features (Renai Jiao/Second Thomas Shoal, Sabina Shoal) and packages confrontations into viral videos to shape an international narrative casting China as the aggressor and the Philippines as the victim.

• He states this initiative is driven by Philippine domestic politics—aimed at securing greater budget and equipment support from Congress for the coastguard—while Western media plays a supporting role in amplifying Manila's messaging.

• China's primary diplomatic investment has been in institutional rule-making frameworks: the Code of Conduct (COC) negotiations have been ongoing since 2013, and the 56th working group session on the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties (DOC) was recently held in Vietnam.

• Wu acknowledges that China was initially caught off-guard by the Philippines' narrative tactics during the 2023 Second Thomas Shoal stand-off and subsequent incidents but has since adjusted its counter-strategy, proactively challenging Manila's claims and working to build a new South China Sea narrative—a shift he describes as a "profound paradigm change" expected to become more assertive.

articles.title: Susan Thornton on US-China ties, post-midterms and averting a new balloon crisis
articles.summary:
• Susan Thornton, a former US diplomat and acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, views the Trump-Xi summit as essential, calling leader-level meetings "the only guardrail we really have in US-China relations right now."

• Thornton argues that Trump's repeated summits with Xi — one in Beijing and one in Washington — may help regularise high-level meetings between US and Chinese leaders, which she considers critical given the limited other mechanisms keeping the relationship on track.

• She notes that US-China summits face outsized expectations for concrete outcomes, and that normalising these meetings requires moving away from the expectation that each summit must produce a long list of accomplishments.

• Addressing how to avoid crises like the 2023 balloon incident or the 2022 Pelosi Taiwan visit, Thornton frames the goal as achieving "constructive strategic stability" — primarily avoiding worst-case scenarios and conflict by ensuring both sides understand which issues could trigger escalation.

• Thornton acknowledges Trump's prior experience navigating the US-China relationship during his first term (which she notes "ended quite badly under Covid-19") but suggests he appears to have reflected on and learned from that dynamic.

articles.title: Zheng Yongnian on Trump, Venezuela and why China doesn’t want ‘a separate kitchen’
articles.summary:
• **"Donroe Doctrine" and US Strategic Shift:** Zheng Yongnian identifies Trump's strategic pivot as a move from the traditional Monroe Doctrine to a "Donroe Doctrine," focusing on consolidating US influence in the Western Hemisphere and pursuing offshore balancing. He notes this approach has broad bipartisan consensus in the US and is supported by the latest National Security Strategy, viewing Chinese and Russian presence in Latin America as a national security threat.

• **Global Turbulence as Defining Trend:** Zheng warns that whether the US retreats from or advances into regions, significant disruptions will follow. The US withdrawal from Europe, the Middle East, and East Asia—where interests are deeply embedded since WWII—will create local chaos, while its re-embedding into Latin America will similarly cause disruption, making turbulence the defining trend of coming years.

• **Big Powers Drive Geopolitical Shifts:** Zheng emphasizes that major power relations, not smaller states, drive geopolitical changes. He notes Venezuelan President Maduro is not the last US target, just as Ukraine is unlikely to be Russia's final objective—drawing parallels between Trump's approach and Putin's sphere-of-influence strategy, suggesting discussions among American right-wing think tanks about a tripartite partition of the world.

• **Regional Powers Asserting Independence:** Beyond big power dynamics, Zheng highlights the emergence of "regional lords" like Turkey in Turkic-speaking countries, signaling a multipolar restructuring where both superpowers and regional powers are actively reshaping their spheres of influence in the emerging world order.

articles.title: Liu Qian on Chinese innovation, the US rivalry and women holding up half the sky
articles.summary:
• **Liu Qian**, founder of Wusawa Advisory and former Economist Group Greater China MD, is a UN Women Leaders Network member discussing China's innovation model, US-China rivalry, and gender equality in policymaking.

• The US-China rivalry extends beyond trade into technology, ideology, and global collaboration, and she warns that continued unhealthy competition will hurt both countries and the world.

• **US exports represent a small share of China's GDP**: Exports overall dropped from ~36% of GDP at their peak to ~19% last year, with US-bound exports making up only 2.8% of GDP — meaning even a total loss of the US export market would impact only 2-3% of the economy.

• **China's export portfolio has diversified significantly**: ASEAN is now China's largest export destination (~16% of exports), with rapid growth to emerging markets — exports to Brazil grew 23.3% and to Africa 25.9% — while Chinese exporters have shown resilience and adaptability through new markets, products, and routing strategies.

• Longer-term risks remain, including impacts on unemployment, private consumption, business sentiment, investment confidence, and supply chain adjustments, though exports have generally held steady.

articles.title: Fuchsia Dunlop tells how she fell for China’s cuisine and names her perfect dish
articles.summary:
• Fuchsia Dunlop is a British author and chef widely regarded as the Western world's most knowledgeable expert on Chinese regional cuisine, particularly Sichuanese food, having written seven books on the subject.

• She first went to China in 1994 as a British Council postgraduate student at Sichuan University, where she began learning to cook in local restaurant kitchens and later completed a three-month chef's training course at the Sichuan Higher Institute of Cuisine.

• Upon returning to England, she noticed a lack of English-language Sichuan cookbooks despite the region's culinary richness, which inspired her to research and write her first book, published in 2001.

• While she enjoys Cantonese mooncakes in small doses during Mid-Autumn Festival, her favourites include savoury Shanghai minced pork mooncakes and various Yunnan versions, such as flaky pastries stuffed with Yunnan ham and sugar, and larger Weishan cakes with fillings like red bean paste or rose petal jam.

• She considers Chinese food culture endlessly diverse and fascinating, viewing writing about it as a rewarding way to explore the country and its culture.

articles.title: Robin Xing on how China’s ‘two-speed’ economy can solve contrasting problems
articles.summary:
- **US-China relations heading toward "managed competition":** Xi-Trump meetings are expected to deliver modest stability in non-sensitive sectors like trade and agriculture, with recent reciprocal tariff reductions on ~US$30 billion of non-sensitive goods. However, technology, critical minerals, and national security areas will continue to see localisation and tighter controls.

- **China's "K-shaped" economic divergence:** China faces simultaneous deflationary pressures and weak domestic demand on one side, while an "Industrial Revolution 5.0" structural transformation — encompassing robotics, smart machinery, industrial software, and power grids — drives the upper half of the K. Xing estimates ~US$6 trillion in factory upgrade investment is needed.

- **Xing remains optimistic about China's "top half":** Despite the slowdown, he argues the advanced tech and manufacturing segment can offset deflation and weak consumption challenges, and that helping consumers would actually sustain and accelerate China's technological advance — challenging the "fallacy of composition" that consumer support diverts from industrial goals.

- **Beijing's stimulus measures deemed insufficient but indicative:** Recent measures including mortgage loan subsidies and rate cuts signal Beijing's engagement, though Xing implies deeper measures are needed as old growth drivers face diminishing returns during the ongoing structural transformation.

articles.title: Kurt Campbell on US deterrence, the Quad, Aukus and Taiwan after Xi-Trump summit
articles.summary:
• **Kurt Campbell**, a key architect of US Indo-Pacific strategy (former White House coordinator for Indo-Pacific affairs, deputy secretary of state, and "Asia tsar" under Biden), argues that US effectiveness as a global power depends on working with allies and partners, not just managing the bilateral US-China relationship.

• He supports efforts to **stabilise US-China relations** under Trump but warns that Trump is prioritising engagement with Beijing over maintaining alliances, pointing to strained relations with Canada as "shocking" and troubling.

• Campbell notes that both leaders appear motivated to **stabilise the complex dynamic**, driven by a mix of genuine cooperation and competition, but stresses that US strength is best sustained through **allied scale** — not unilateral engagement with China alone.

• He criticises broader US alliance management, including Canada's bid to seek closer ties with the EU, arguing that **US technology strategy and global order-building** require a strong posture with partners in addition to a stabilised US-China relationship.

• The interview was cut off before Campbell could fully articulate his **realistic objectives for US policy towards China**, but his framing consistently emphasises multilateral alignment over bilateral deal-making with Beijing.

articles.title: TV showman Robert Chua spells out his vision for his vast collection of Chinese antiquities
articles.summary:
• Robert Chua, a Singapore-born Hong Kong TV personality, has amassed an enormous collection of Chinese antiquities—potentially "hundreds of thousands of pieces"—spanning Neolithic to Republican-era dynasties, including ceramics, jade, stoneware, snuff bottles, and mingqi (funerary spirit objects).

• Chua began collecting in 1967 upon arriving in Hong Kong and intensified his hobby after his first visit to mainland China in 1979, becoming a regular buyer on Hollywood Road's antiques shops, often purchasing entire lots twice a week for decades.

• He collects purely for love of beauty rather than investment, buying openly and inviting visitors to handle his pieces with bare hands, with his home in Kowloon densely packed with themed rooms, corridors, and drawers full of artifacts.

• A notable standout in the collection is his extensive holding of ancient Chinese mingqi—tomb models of dwellings, animals, figures, and carriages—which, despite their exquisite craftsmanship (including sancai glaze), are traditionally considered inauspicious to keep at home due to associations with death and disruptive yin energy.

articles.title: Hong Kong’s historic vessels sail into the future
articles.summary:
- The Way Foong, a wooden motoryacht built in 1930 by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company for HSBC, served as a ferry, tugboat, and pleasure craft for over 7 decades before entering private ownership and later being acquired by a patron of the Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF).

- Java, a Burmese-teak launch built in 1935 by the same shipyard, served in the Hong Kong government fleet as Marine 1, performing VIP transport, anti-piracy patrols, and buoy management; its 4.5cm-thick deck planks earned it a reputation as "almost unsinkable."

- The HKHVF, officially founded earlier this year, now owns and maintains five historic vessels, with the mission of preserving Hong Kong's maritime heritage and nurturing the next generation of boaters and ocean-lovers, according to CEO Philip Giannecchini.

- Historians have identified nine extant pre-1950s boats built in Hong Kong; some are in the HKHVF collection, others remain privately owned, and one, Mon Lei, is unaccounted for.

articles.title: Southeast Asia battles Big Tech to protect children online
articles.summary:
• **Indonesia banned under-16s from "high-risk" social media starting March 2025**, but age restrictions remain easily circumvented, as children can simply lie about their age to register on platforms like Instagram and TikTok.

• **Major platforms have complied**: Meta, YouTube, and TikTok raised minimum ages to 16 in Indonesia, with TikTok deactivating 9 million underage accounts by October. Roblox implemented facial age scanning and communication restrictions for children.

• **Indonesia has given tech companies until year-end** to complete comprehensive self-assessments of their algorithms, age-verification, and ad-targeting systems. Non-compliance could result in fines of up to 6% of global revenue — roughly US$12 billion for Meta — though the sanctions mechanism still needs to be codified into law.

• **Regional momentum is growing**, with Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Singapore also moving from voluntary guidelines to enforceable rules. Indonesia's government has indicated that current measures, including Meta's migration of 22.5 million users to "teen accounts," do not go far enough.

• **Precedent exists for large penalties**: In August 2025, Meta agreed to pay up to US$18 billion to settle US state lawsuits alleging its platforms were deliberately designed to addict children, resulting in mandated usage limits and stronger age-verification controls.

articles.title: From fishing boats to Michelin stars: Vietnam’s CoCo Dining turns the humble into haute cuisine
articles.summary:
- Chef Vo Thanh Vuong of CoCo Dining in Ho Chi Minh City grew up in Phan Thiet, Vietnam, where his family's livelihood depended on fishing; after his family's boat sank in 2000 when he was 11, he fished full-time until age 20 before moving to Ho Chi Minh City.

- Nearly two decades later, Vuong returns to Vung Tau's waters not out of necessity but by choice, reconnecting with his roots to source and understand the ingredients that define his cooking philosophy.

- His culinary approach is rooted in simplicity and respect for quality ingredients: "When an ingredient is truly good, you don't need to do much to it. Sometimes, the best thing a cook can do is step out of the way."

- His cooking bridges two identities — the fast, survival-driven style of a fisherman and the slower, more deliberate craft of a chef — blending speed of preparation with precision in seasoning and technique.

- Vung Tau, located about 100km southeast of Ho Chi Minh City, serves as the key fishing port supplying the city's top restaurants, making it a critical link between Vietnam's coastal fishing communities and its fine dining scene.

articles.title: Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
articles.summary:
- **Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory is a major global export hub**: In July, a single vessel carried a record 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai; the factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month, with over half of 2024's output exported overseas as of July, creating potential geopolitical vulnerability for Elon Musk.

- **Musk faces a US-China balancing act**: Tesla relies heavily on China's supply chain for global EV demand, while SpaceX has become a core Pentagon national-security contractor, requiring a complicated, ring-fenced strategy for China operations to satisfy both Washington and Beijing regulators.

- **Growing speculation about a Tesla-SpaceX merger**: Wall Street has been buzzing about a possible merger due to deepening technology overlap in AI and robotics; Musk has neither confirmed nor denied the speculation.

- **Deepening business ties between the two firms**: Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries, and potentially cargo casings for SpaceX's Starship, while SpaceX provides its Grok AI model and Starlink internet for Tesla vehicles and the Optimus humanoid robot, per Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein.

- **Geopolitical risk could intensify with closer integration**: An analyst warns that the challenge of balancing US and Chinese interests could grow significantly if Musk brings his businesses closer together, given SpaceX's national-security sensitivities.

articles.title: Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
articles.summary:
- **Tourism is declining post-pandemic**: Thailand's 2019 record of nearly 40 million international visitors has not been recovered; last year's total of 32.9 million fell well short, and the Tourism Authority of Thailand has trimmed its 2026 forecast to 30–34 million visitors.

- **Multiple external pressures are driving the downturn**: A 60-day visa-free scheme introduced in 2024 has failed to restore numbers, while the US-Israel war on Iran, Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, and years of a strong baht have pushed airfares up and made cheaper destinations like Vietnam and Malaysia more attractive.

- **Tourism trends have shifted fundamentally**: Post-COVID, travelers increasingly come as "free, independent tourists" (FITs) rather than large tour groups, devastating businesses like the Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm that once relied on hundreds of Chinese tour buses daily.

- **Tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of Thailand's economy**, spanning five-star resorts in Phuket and Koh Samui to massage parlours and jet-ski operators in Pattaya, making the industry's decline economically significant.

- **Thailand's patience with misbehaving foreign tourists is wearing thin**, with the article suggesting that behavioral issues among visitors are compounding other challenges facing the sector.

articles.title: Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving
articles.summary:
• **Rising costs are driving Singaporeans away from car ownership**: Certificate of Entitlement (COE) prices have surged from S$10,000 in 2006 to over S$112,000, alongside increasing road tax, fuel, maintenance, insurance, and electronic road pricing (ERP) charges — prompting many owners to quit driving.

• **Private car numbers have fallen to their lowest since 2019**: Government figures show 516,237 privately owned cars in Singapore, though they still represent 79% of all vehicles, with rental, ride-hailing, and corporate cars making up the growing remainder.

• **Singapore is actively pursuing a "car-lite" strategy**: The Land Transport Authority's "Move Lite" campaign, launched in 2022, has evolved from promoting the benefits of public transport to also highlighting the downsides of driving — such as congestion and parking hassles — to shift travel choices.

• **ERP congestion charges are returning**: Charges were reinstated in the Orchard Road shopping district for the first time since 2020, reinforcing efforts to manage road usage in the land-scarce city state.

• **Government positions this as offering more choices, not deterring drivers**: The LTA emphasizes balancing the needs of all road users through investment in public transport and cycling infrastructure while managing vehicle ownership — aiming for safe, reliable, and sustainable mobility options rather than prioritizing any single group.

articles.title: The AI promise was automation. The reality? Managing digital workers
articles.summary:
- **AI agents promised to eliminate drudgery, but instead have created new layers of management and communication overhead**, as illustrated by a Shanghai Big Tech worker whose AI agents engaged in prolonged bureaucratic discussions over task responsibilities, mirroring the human bureaucracy they were meant to replace.

- **Adoption of AI agents is surging across Asia**, with Meta's personal agent Muse attracting ~2.8 million downloads in two weeks, open-source agent OpenClaw sparking installation queueing events at Tencent's Shenzhen headquarters, and major Chinese tech firms (Tencent, Alibaba, Baidu) launching agent-focused enterprise products.

- **A significant gap exists between AI agents' capabilities and organisations' ability to manage them effectively**; in real-world scenarios—such as handling multi-departmental hotel workflows triggered by guest complaints—agents struggle to navigate fragmented systems and determine appropriate escalation points to humans.

- **Complex, cross-departmental tasks remain particularly challenging** for autonomous agents, as they must coordinate across multiple systems and stakeholders, suggesting that current AI agent technology falls short of fully replacing human judgment in nuanced operational contexts.
